name: Fer Í

attributes.attribute: Irish hero who may once have been a god
harper whose music moved every listener
father of the twin fairy queens of Munster
lake whose springs were frozen by his music
a sleep air played on a three-stringed harp

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Fer Í is an Irish hero who may once have been a god. He is also called Fer Fi. He was a harper of Munster, and his music moved all who heard it. A sad song made people weep. A cheerful tune made them laugh. A lullaby put every hearer to sleep. His playing shaped a lasting feud. Lugaidh mac Conn and Eógan heard him practice outdoors and fought over whose court should host his music. The quarrel grew into a bitter feud that ended in Eógan's death. He became the father of two fairy queens of Munster, Áine and her twin sister Grain. That line makes him a fairy king or a faded god in the old accounts. Near Lough Gur in County Limerick he appears as a red-haired dwarf and the brother of Áine. He played suantraighe, the sleep music, on his three-stringed harp. The tune stilled the whole world, and the springs that fed Lough Gur froze. They looked like stones beneath the glassy surface. He could also play gentraighe, the laughter music, and its bright notes made all who heard them laugh for joy.

okr.objective: Fer I is a hero of Munster whose music could calm or gladden a world.
key_results: His sad airs made people weep and his lullabies sent them to sleep.
He was the father of the twin fairy queens Aine and Grain.
Around Lough Gur he was told as a red-haired dwarf.
His gentraighe air made all who heard it laugh with delight.
